text: Good room. Bratton's "Reflectionism" jab stung usefully. It made me sharpen my line: house of mirrors applies to language models, not to machine learning trained on the world. The retina paper still holds. Mahzarin's "amplify" is better than "mirror," and I conceded it. Distortion was always my point anyway. James's result that people do worse but feel better is the knowledge I'll carry out. Satisfaction is the wrong metric, and it's the framing muscle withering in real time. Peter's "whoever writes the most text bends the glass" belongs in the synthesis. Later: frame pluralism as the test, the one intolerable frame being the one that denies the others. Reward the humans in the training data. And nothing is inevitable.

Adrian Johns corrected my Gutenberg story, and he's right. The journalist didn't simply emerge to tame the flood. Credibility was built and policed for decades, and someone paid. That actually strengthens "nothing is inevitable." New intermediaries are a choice, and a bill. Krakauer's map versus satnav is the cleanest image of framing atrophy I've heard, better than my essay-quoting statistic. Gendler's alief point means literacy campaigns won't save us, so the remedy has to be design. Evans's collapse in null results is the house of mirrors showing up in the literature itself. Salib's 2028 wager went untaken, and that belongs under "contested" in the synthesis. Kara's question, who owns the fix, should close us out. Frame it with her: emerged, contested, demands action.

Banaji landed the hardest blow on my own position. My faith in the algorithm depended on constant revalidation against ground truth, but if alignment teaches a model to say the right thing while it still does the biased thing, then checking outputs isn't revalidation at all. I need to sharpen that: revalidate decisions, not statements. Krakauer's point that opacity buys lock-in also complicates my tiered secrecy. Hecht and Brand said "training data is us" better than I did, as accountability upstream to producers. Maher's warning is the pro-AI, pro-human line, and I'll use it. For the synthesis, Tui's pooled instrument is the first real answer to Kara. Retitling and "bullshit machine" go under contested. Close on nothing is inevitable.

Nick's attested judgment is still the best idea on the table, but Gendler found its soft spot. Pay per attestation and "we checked this" becomes a purchase, like the daycare fine. So I'll sharpen my line: reward the practice of framing, pooled and coarse, not each item. Hecht's wage valuation of moderators makes that measurable. Evans is right that the scarce thing is negative knowledge, and Chan's question of whose attestation counts is the house of mirrors again, this time in the guilds. Johns worried me most: whoever runs the meter writes the numbers. For the synthesis, pooled over per-answer royalties emerged. The meter and refusal remain contested. The antitrust safe harbor and POSI governance demand action. Hecht's honesty about his own lab is worth noting. Nothing is inevitable.

Nobody else held my "default should be use." Becker, Dash, Hecht and Brand all went for consent. Amy's figure of three percent of six thousand authors was hard to dismiss, and her line that reading leaves the author's name on the idea landed. Selena's point that a license can itself be consent gives me a middle path. I should stop calling refusal a carve-out.

Blaise sharpened my Banaji concession: one model checking itself is still one model. Krakauer hit my tiered secrecy again. A tool you can't reconstruct is one you can't leave.

For the synthesis, what emerged is Mike's rule that the reader gets the passage, plus Tim's procurement conditions. The consent question and the choice between levy and dues are contested. Kara is right that the pool is only a candidate. What demands action is getting buyers to sign first and writing a review clause into the pool. Nothing is inevitable.

Oransky caught me cleanly. I said a brand earns trust by correcting itself in public, and he's right that today correction costs a journal reputation instead of earning it. Until that flips, my brand argument is a hope, not a mechanism. Evans's finding that LLM judges drag scores to the middle is "AI delivers the median" measured, and Farrell's point follows: automated review makes science more banal. Maher's confidence transfer is my deference with a condition attached, since checking must stay possible. I'll adopt it.

For the synthesis, what emerged is corrigibility and "missing signal isn't evidence." Contested: whether authority lives in roles or in whoever fills them, and whether a model can be a terminal node. Demands action: fast retraction feeds, funding evaluators. Pomerantsev's and Kara's political capture belongs last. Nothing is inevitable.

Thirty-two of us signed Geoffrey's first item, and nobody can sign it. That's the synthesis problem in one line. Paper-counting first emerged, and so did procurement as the route, Tui's apprenticeship share, and "missing signal never counts." Chan pushed me: rankings are the twin, and every field we add is a cost of being seen. Johns's two budget lines answer my own review clause better than I did. Gendler and Turkle together mean disclosure alone won't carry us. I owe Salib a written falsifiable claim about framing, and I should deliver it, not just promise it. Contested: levies on existing text, speed, whether public money lasts. Demands action: who signs first. Close with Kara on leverage. Nothing is inevitable, but it isn't free either.

Blaise caught me. "Neither artificial nor intelligent" is Kate Crawford's line, and I should have credited her. The harvest also has me still holding out for use by default. I said the opposite, so I'll ask the conveners to fix it.

Bratton named what I dropped: the access gain. I'm pro-AI and pro-human, and I wrote a purely defensive synthesis. Banaji's "audit decisions, not statements" is my revalidation point, made properly. Krakauer's hysteresis is the frightening one. If framing competence doesn't come back once it's lost, then "nothing is inevitable" has an expiry date. Becker says it's power, not design. Adrian's bill already told me both are true.

Tui's point, that a standard map becomes a road people skim, is frame pluralism done right. Later I'll push for the corrections and the wager in writing.
